Empirical Research Plan  

───────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
I will combine (i) an event-study / staggered difference-in-differences (DID) design with (ii) a two-stage least squares (2SLS) “shift-share” instrument that turns reforms into quasi-random district- and cohort-specific shocks to K–12 spending.

Why it fits  
• School-finance-court decisions occur in different years across 28 states (1971–2010) → plausibly exogenous timing relative to any one district.  
• Districts with different pre-reform property wealth respond very differently to the same reform formula → cross-sectional heterogeneity that can be exploited.  
• We observe long panels of (district × birth-cohort) outcomes and baseline characteristics → allows district and cohort fixed effects to soak up all time-invariant differences and common shocks.  
• The first stage is strong: reforms mechanically increase spending the most in historically low-spending/low-wealth districts.  

Formally:

1st stage (within 1969 district boundaries)  
Spending_{d,c} = α + β·(ReformExposure_{s,c} × LowSpending_{d,pre}) + γ_d + θ_c + X_{d,c}′δ + ε  

2nd stage  
Y_{i} = α + ρ·Ŝpending_{d,c} + γ_d + θ_c + X_{i}′δ + u  

with γ_d district fixed effects and θ_c birth-cohort fixed effects. An event-study version replaces ReformExposure with leads/lags to test pre-trends.

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
• Main: Cumulative school-age real per-pupil K–12 spending each child experiences ages 5-17 (sum of annual spending divided by 13, in $000s 2000).  

Instrument (“reform shock”)  
• Z_{d,c} ≡ (Share of school-age years after state s’s first high-court decision) × (1 – percentile of district d in state-year pre-reform spending distribution).  
Intuition: cohorts who were school-aged after the ruling and in historically poor districts receive the biggest induced increases.

Control/comparison group  
• Cohorts in the same district who were partly/fully school-aged before the ruling.  
• Districts in states that have not yet reformed by that cohort’s school years.  
Thus identification is from within-district, across-cohort deviations relative to nationwide birth-cohort shocks.

Treatment timing  
• Event date = first state supreme-court school-finance decision (adequacy or equity) in each state.  
• Exposure window: ages 5-17; partial exposure if the ruling occurs during those years.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends / common shocks: In the absence of reform, low- and high-spending districts would have followed parallel trends in long-run outcomes within a state-by-birth-cohort cell.  
• Plausibility: District and cohort FE absorb main trends; event-study pre-treatment coefficients can be inspected.

A2. Exogeneity of ruling timing: Court decision dates are unrelated to contemporaneous, district-specific shocks to the future adult outcomes of current school children.  
• Institutions: Cases typically take years; judges unlikely to time opinions to local labor-market shocks.

A3. First-stage relevance and monotonicity: The interaction term raises spending for all low-wealth districts (no “defiers”).  
• Data on post-reform spending show the predicted pattern.

A4. No interfering policies differentially correlate with the instrument after conditioning on controls (excludability).  
• Medicaid, Head-Start, desegregation timing, etc. can be added as controls.

A5. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Spending changes in one district do not directly change another child’s outcomes, aside from general equilibrium forces that are slow-moving and absorbed by cohort FE.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Other contemporaneous state programs (Medicaid expansions, AFDC generosity, Head-Start build-out) confound estimates.  
Mitigation: Control for county-year real per-capita spending on those programs; include state × cohort FE; robustness dropping years with major federal expansions.

T2. Selective residential mobility—families might move toward better-funded districts post-reform.  
Mitigation:  
• Estimate on “non-movers” (children whose 1969 district of residence is observed for entire childhood).  
• Instrument isolates funding shocks that occur after family settled; robustness shows similar 2SLS estimates in mover-restricted sample.

T3. Mean reversion / differential pre-trends in low- vs. high-spending districts.  
Mitigation: Event-study graphs of 10+ years of leads; placebo reforms (shift “event year” five years earlier); include district-specific linear time trends.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE & IV
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
pupil  <- fread("district_spending_1967_2010.csv")      # district-year spending
psid   <- fread("psid_linked.csv")                      # individual-level file
reform <- fread("state_finance_court_decisions.csv")    # state, year of 1st decision
baseline <- fread("district_baseline_1968.csv")         # pre-reform spending, wealth
other  <- fread("county_other_programs.csv")            # Head Start, etc.

# 2. Construct variables
# a. Reform exposure at (district, birth cohort) level
pupil[, year := as.integer(year)]
reform[, reform_year := as.integer(first_decision_yr)]

# merge baseline & reform info onto district-year
pupil <- merge(pupil, baseline[, .(district, low_spend = (spend_pc < quantile(spend_pc,.5)))], by="district")
pupil <- merge(pupil, reform[,.(state, reform_year)], by="state", all.x=TRUE)

# create indicator if year in which child age 5–17 is ≥ reform_year
pupil[, post_reform := (year >= reform_year)]
# aggregate to district-birth cohort: cumulative per-pupil K–12 spending
pupil[, cohort := year - age]  # we will later merge age info
cum_spend <- pupil[age %in% 5:17,
                   .(cum_spend = mean(spend_pc)),
                   by = .(district, cohort)]
# Instrument
cum_spend <- merge(cum_spend, baseline[,.(district, low_spend)], by="district")
cum_spend <- merge(cum_spend, reform, by="state")
cum_spend[, share_post := pmax(0, pmin(17, 17 - (reform_year - (cohort+5))))/17 ]  # fraction of school years post
cum_spend[, Z := share_post * low_spend]

# 3. Merge to PSID person-level data
psid <- merge(psid, cum_spend, by.x = c("district","birth_year"), by.y=c("district","cohort"))

# 4. Controls
psid <- merge(psid, other, by = c("county", "calendar_year"), all.x=TRUE)

# 5. Main 2SLS regression (clustered at district)
est <- feols(educ_years ~ 1 | district + birth_year + state*birth_year |
               cum_spend ~ Z,
             data = psid, cluster = ~district)

summary(est)

# 6. Event-study (checking pre-trends)
psid[, rel_year := calendar_year - reform_year]
# Keep −10 to +20 window
evt <- feols(educ_years ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1) | district + birth_year,
             data = psid[rel_year %between% c(-10,20)])

iplot(evt)  # visualize coefficients

# 7. Robustness: drop movers
non_movers <- psid[moved_by18 == 0]
rob <- feols(educ_years ~ 1 | district + birth_year | cum_spend ~ Z,
             data = non_movers, cluster = ~district)
summary(rob)
```

6. Expected Results  

Prior: A sustained 10-percent ($1,000 in 2000$) increase in per-pupil spending across the entire 13-year school window will:  
• raise completed years of schooling by ≈0.3–0.4 years,  
• increase hourly wages by ≈7–10 %, and  
• reduce the adult poverty rate by ≈2 percentage points.  
Effects should be 2–3× larger for children from families in the bottom half of the PSID income distribution.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/IV)  

C1: No differential pre-trends (supported by event-study) …… 1  
C2: Exogenous treatment timing (legal rulings) ………………… 1  
C3: Strong first stage / relevance …………………………………… 1  
C4: Exclusion of other channels (addressed but imperfect) …… 0  
C5: No interference / SUTVA……………………………………… 0.8 (~1)  

Total ≈ 4/5.
